big: Rohan's father passed away. The family filed a claim, and it was rejected. The reason: he had not told the insurer that he smoked. A few seconds on a form had changed everything.

lines: What matters most when buying, and what happens when the family needs to claim?
Tell the insurer everything honestly, name a nominee, keep the policy papers safe and review it after big life events.

title: Buying and claiming
stops: Tell the insurer every fact that matters
A nominee is optional and never needs updating
You can review a new policy within a set window
Claim settlement ratio is the only thing to check
caps: Material disclosure means telling the insurer every fact that could affect its decision.
A nominee receives the claim, and should be updated after life events.
After you receive the policy, there is a review window to cancel and get the premium back, less small deductions.
A high claim ratio is a good sign, but read the terms too.

rows: Health, smoking, other policies and income, all honestly
Name one, and update it after marriage or a child
At least 15 days after the policy arrives to cancel if unhappy
Check the claim settlement ratio, and read the terms
note: The claim settlement ratio is the share of claims an insurer paid out of those received.

q: Rohan smokes occasionally but ticks 'non-smoker' to get a lower premium. What is the risk?
opts: None, since the insurer will not check
The policy simply costs a little more
The claim may be rejected later, for hiding a material fact
The sum assured is cut in half at the time of the claim
why: Insurers can investigate at claim time, so false answers are a real risk.
The consequence is not a small price rise, it can be a refusal of the claim.
Hiding a material fact such as smoking can lead to a rejected claim.
There is no automatic halving. The risk is rejection.

q: Meena got married and had a child. Her policy still names her old nominee. What should she do?
opts: Nothing, since the nominee stays valid for all time
Cancel the policy and buy a new one every time
Tell the neighbours who the nominee is
Update the nominee so the claim goes to the right person
why: Life changes, so the nomination should be kept up to date.
Cancelling restarts underwriting and costs more, and is not needed.
Telling neighbours does not change the policy record.
Updating avoids confusion and delay for the family at the time of a claim.

q: Dadi receives her policy and finds the terms differ from what she was told. What can she do?
opts: Use the review window to cancel and recover the premium
Nothing at all, since the premium has already been paid up
Wait ten years and then complain only after that long
Sell the policy on to a friend who agrees to take it
why: A review window after receipt lets her cancel and recover the premium, less small deductions.
Paying does not remove her right to review the terms after the policy arrives.
Delay makes it harder, since the review window is short and closes.
Policies are not usually sold on to friends, so the window is the proper route.

q: Which insurer record is worth checking, along with reading the terms?
opts: The number of branch offices it has in your own city today
The claim settlement ratio, claims paid versus received
The colour and the design of its printed policy brochure
The number of agents that it employs across the whole country
why: Offices do not show how claims are actually paid out to families.
A higher ratio suggests a better claim-paying record, though the terms still matter.
Design says nothing about how the insurer treats its claims.
Agent numbers do not show how the insurer handles claims.

pts: Tell the insurer every material fact honestly when you buy.
Name a nominee and update it after life events.
Use the review window, and check the claim settlement ratio.
